latest_release.name: v2026.11.8: Bootstrap settings plugins, block edits in bootstrap files, and argv in command wrappers
latest_release.body:
This release extends `mise bootstrap` with experimental settings plugins, system-wide plugin directories, block edits for system files, and repositories and hooks in `mise bootstrap plan`. macOS preferences move to `[bootstrap.settings.macos]`. Command wrappers can now read the user's arguments, and a new setting keeps private GitHub repos off mise-versions. It also fixes problems in lockfiles, hook-env performance, tasks and backends.

## Added

### Bootstrap

- **Bootstrap settings plugins (experimental).** A plugin can now apply one program's or desktop's settings from a `[bootstrap.settings.<plugin>]` section. The plugin reads and writes values, and mise compares them and writes only the keys that differ. A new `settings` bootstrap part runs after tools and package plugins. It works with `--only settings` and `--skip settings`, and the new `mise bootstrap settings status` and `mise bootstrap settings apply [--dry-run]` commands manage it directly. If a section's plugin is missing or can't run on this OS, mise skips the section and lists it as a follow-up. Settings plugins need `experimental = true` and are not yet included in `mise bootstrap status` or `plan`. [#15621](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15621) (@jdx)

  ```toml
  [bootstrap.settings.omarchy.appearance]
  blur = true
  blur_strength = 4
  ```

- **System plugin directories.** A distro or admin can install bootstrap package manager plugins once for every user on the machine. After the user's own plugins directory, mise searches `/usr/share/mise/plugins` and then `$MISE_SYSTEM_DATA_DIR/plugins` (default `/usr/local/share/mise/plugins`). `MISE_SYSTEM_PLUGINS_DIRS` replaces this list. These plugins need no `[bootstrap.plugins]` entry. A user plugin with the same name overrides a system plugin. mise uses a system plugin only if root or the current user owns it and its group and other users can't write to it. System plugin directories are ignored on Windows. `mise plugins ls` labels these plugins `(system)`, and `mise plugins update` and `uninstall` skip them. [#15620](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15620) (@jdx)

- **Block edits in `[bootstrap.files]`.** An entry can now manage a marked block inside a file mise doesn't own, such as `/etc/hosts`, without replacing the rest of the file. mise uses `sudo` only when the current user can't make the change. If the file is missing, mise creates it with just the block. `block` can't be combined with `source`, `content`, `replace`, `remove_empty` or `state = "absent"`, and you have to remove a block by hand for now. [#15650](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15650) (@jdx, @aacebedo)

  ```toml
  [bootstrap.files."/etc/hosts"]
  id = "dev"
  block = """
  127.0.0.1 dev.local
  127.0.0.1 api.local
  """
  ```

- **Repositories and hooks in `mise bootstrap plan`.** Repositories show as `create`, `update` or `unchanged`. A repository with local changes or conflicts shows as `unknown`, and `--detailed-exitcode` fails on it. Hooks appear with a new `run` action and a `hook_phase` field. They don't count as changes for `--detailed-exitcode`. The JSON `summary` gains a `run` count. Repository credentials are left out of the output. [#15653](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15653) (@jdx, @azohra)

### Tools, tasks and dotfiles

- **`argv` in command wrapper templates.** A wrapper's `args` and `env` templates can now use `argv`, the list of arguments the user passed after the command name. The user's arguments are still forwarded unchanged after the wrapper's own `args`. `command` can't use `argv`. [#15655](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15655) (@jdx, @andersonkrs)

  ```toml
  [wrappers.rails]
  command = "fnox"
  args = ["--profile={{ 'test' if argv[0] == 'test' else 'development' }}", "exec", "--", "rails"]
  ```

- **`versions_host_exclude` setting.** This setting takes case-insensitive `owner/repo` glob patterns. mise looks up matching `github:` repos directly on GitHub instead of sending their names to mise-versions, and eve

## What is mise? mise (pronounced "meez", short for _mise-en-place_) manages a project's dev tools, environment variables, and tasks from one `mise.toml` that works across your shell, editor, and CI: ```toml [tools] node = "24" python = "3.14" rust = "stable" "cargo:cargo-nextest" = "0.9" "github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "15" "npm:prettier" = "3" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" _.file = ".env" _.path = "./node_modules/.bin" [tasks.build] description = "Build the application" run = "npm run build" [tasks.test] description = "Run the test suite" depends = ["build"] run = "pytest && npm test" ``` - Install [dev tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/) such as Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, and Terraform from a [registry of 1,000+ tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) or directly from [backends](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/) like GitHub releases, Aqua, Cargo, npm, and PyPI, with separate versions per project. - Load [environment variables](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/), `.env` files, `PATH` entries, virtualenvs, and [secrets](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/secrets/) automatically as you enter a directory. - Run [tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/) defined in `mise.toml` or as scripts in `mise-tasks/`, with dependencies, parallel execution, file watching, and the project's tools and environment already configured. - Set up a machine with [`mise bootstrap`](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [`mise dot apply`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) to apply system packages, dotfiles, Git repositories, macOS defaults, and background services. Adopt only the parts you need. Start with a single tool or task, and keep any existing `.tool-versions` files as they are; mise also reads `.nvmrc`, `.python-version`, and other [idiomatic version files](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/versions.html#idiomatic-version-files) once enabled. [![Demo of mise managing tools](./docs/tapes/demo.gif)](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html) See the [demo transcript](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html#transcript) for the commands shown above. ## Quickstart ### 1. Install mise On macOS or Linux: ```sh curl -fsSL https://mise.run | sh ~/.local/bin/mise --version ``` On Windows, run `winget install jdx.mise`. For Homebrew, apt, dnf, Scoop, and other package managers, see [Installing mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html). The installer places the binary at `~/.local/bin/mise`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH` yet, run `~/.local/bin/mise` in place of `mise` until you activate mise in step 4. ### 2. Run a tool without changing your shell ```sh mise exec node@24 -- node --version # v24.x.x ``` [`mise exec`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/exec.html) downloads Node.js 24 if needed and runs the command after `--` with that version on `PATH`. Your shell and config files stay untouched. ### 3. Configure a project Create a project directory, select Node.js 24, set an environment variable, and add a task: ```sh mkdir my-project && cd my-project mise use node@24 mise set NODE_ENV=development mise tasks add hello -- node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)" ``` These commands install Node.js 24 and write `mise.toml`: ```toml [tools] node = "24" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" [tasks.hello] run = 'node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)"' ``` Run the task with [`mise run`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/run.html): ```sh mise run hello # [hello] $ node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)" # v24.x.x development ``` Commit `mise.toml` so teammates and CI get the same setup when they run `mise install` or `mise run`. `"24"` requests the latest release in the Node.js 24 series; run `mise lock` to record exact versions and checksums in a [lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html), or `mise use --global node@24` to set a personal default in `~/.config/mise/config.toml`. ### 4. Activate mise in your shell (optional) Shell activation updates `PATH` and project environment variables whenever you change directories, so you can invoke `node` directly without `mise exec`. If you installed with `mise.run`, run the command for your shell once, then open a new terminal: ```sh # bash echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc # zsh echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)"' >> "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc" # fish mkdir -p ~/.config/fish echo '~/.local/bin/mise activate fish | source' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish ``` If a package manager installed mise, use `mise` in place of `~/.local/bin/mise`. With Homebrew, fish activates mise without this step. For PowerShell, Nushell, Elvish, Xonsh, and IDE or CI shims, see [Shell setup](https://mise.jdx.dev/shell-setup.html) and [Shims](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html). ## Everyday commands | Command | Action | | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `mise use node@24` | Install a tool and record it in the current project's `mise.toml` | | `mise use --global node@24` | Install a tool and set it as your global default | | `mise install` | Install all tools declared in the active config files | | `mise exec -- ` | Run a command with the project's tools and environment | | `mise run ` | Run a project task with its dependencies, tools, and environment | | `mise set KEY=value` | Set an environment variable in `mise.toml` | | `mise env` | Print the resolved environment variables and `PATH` changes | | `mise ls --current` | List the tool versions active in the current directory | | `mise outdated` | List tools with newer releases than the installed version | | `mise upgrade` | Install those newer releases | | `mise lock` | Write exact tool versions and checksums to `mise.lock` | | `mise config ls` | Show the config files loaded for the current directory | | `mise doctor` | Check your mise installation, shell activation, and configuration | ## Set up a machine with mise bootstrap Beyond project directories, `~/.config/mise/config.toml` can declare the state of your machine: ```toml [bootstrap.packages] "apt:build-essential" = "latest" "brew:jq" = "latest" [bootstrap.repos] "~/src/app" = { url = "https://github.com/you/app.git" } [dotfiles] "~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track" } ``` Preview and apply the configuration, or bootstrap a new machine directly from a Git repository: ```sh mise bootstrap --dry-run mise bootstrap mise bootstrap --adopt you/dotfiles ``` See [Bootstrap](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [Dotfiles](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) for supported package managers, dotfile tracking and templating, services, and remote SSH targets. ## Get help - Report bugs in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/jdx/mise/issues). Check [Troubleshooting](https://mise.jdx.dev/troubleshooting.html) first, and include the command you ran, a minimal `mise.toml`, the expected and actual behavior, and your `mise doctor` output after reviewing it for private details. - Ask questions and share ideas in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions). - Chat with the community on [Discord](https://discord.gg/mABnUDvP57). For security reports and other inquiries, see [Contact](https://mise.jdx.dev/contact.html). ## Special thanks
